Nine thousand gold. Maybe nine and a half. I don't check the exact number. My mouse has a chipped button and I've pressed it so many times tonight the plastic shines.

"Twenty-six twelve," Moth says, before I've taken a step out of the fountain. "Baron buff on them, one fifty-eight left on it. Talon flash down forty more seconds. Pyke flash up at twenty-seven even."

"Noted," I say. I buy nothing. I have a full build — Edge of Night, Youmuu's, Collector, Infinity, Dominik's, and a tear-shaped hole where a defensive item would go if I were a coward. One combo or I die. That's not a build, it's a personality.

Their whole push has stalled at the river mouth — they can't siege, they never could, that's their whole problem and they don't know it yet. Draven has to catch his axes. It's not a choice; the game takes damage away from him if he doesn't, and no Draven in the history of the game has ever willingly done less damage. So when his axe spins out to the far side of his pink ward — past it, a good forty units past it, near the rock where our ward used to be — he steps.

Past the ward. Into the dark.

I'm already there. Thrill of the Hunt, four ferocity, camouflage, and the game tells me where he is.

"Draven walking up," Moth says, but he's late by half a second, and it doesn't matter, because I've already pressed.

The leap is the whole champion. There's no second half. I land on him with five ferocity and the combo goes through my fingers in under a second — Q, empowered Q, the bola, the Collector's threshold. Draven's health bar goes from full to a number I don't read, and then there's a pink mist where the most arrogant man on the server used to be standing.

**Sable has slain Draven!**

Six hundred gold, plus a bounty on top of it. My jaw clicks.

Corporal Deeds came at noon, which was twenty minutes after Otho had told him to.

He descended the stairs sideways, holding a clipboard out from his body as a man holds a lantern in a cave, and he was wearing half a uniform with great formality. He saluted. Otho, who had never in his life been saluted, nodded at him and said, "Hurt your arm?"

"Nothing of the sort. I have brought the requisition."

"Requisition for what?"

"For the raid." Deeds set the clipboard on the bench and turned it, and it was a form, and the form had been filled out in a hand so small and neat it looked printed. "Offensive action, one, in triplicate. There is a section for armament, a section for transportation, and a section for expected casualties, which I have left in pencil. The fourth copy is to be retained by yourself and filed within the unit."

"Unit."

"Us."

"We haven't got any ammunition," Otho said.

"No."

"At all?"

"Nil," Deeds said, and indicated a box. "I have it written here. I've been writing it here for six months. The county militia's stores are in a barn that I no longer hold a requisition for, which is a technical matter, and the technical matter is that the barn belongs to the Walker brothers and they have opinions." He stood very straight. "I should note, for the form, that this unit's transport is one bicycle cart."

"I'm aware."

"And that you cannot evacuate a community of forty on one bicycle cart. I have run that calculation. I have submitted it. It was returned for a signature."

So it was the whole of Bracken Hollow, and there wasn't one of them who had said a word about a different way out. That was the thing about the Hollow, Otho thought. It was too small to run from and too big to carry.

"You've said that about a road eleven times." She did not move her hand. "Otho. I know why you said yes."

"You don't."

"You've got a cellar nobody enters and a batch that pulls the dead from three counties, and you've been down here drinking alone for a month, and she came in and handed you a reason." Sable's voice did not rise. It got quieter and went further in, like a nail driven slow. "You didn't say yes because you've got a nose. You said yes because it's a prettier grave than a bottle and it's got a purpose printed on it. A man like you — you'd rather die requisitioned. Well. You'll die the way the rest of us do, which is stupid and early and in company, and I am not going to stand in your cellar and hold your coat while you arrange it."

The cellar was very quiet. Lottie's stone had stopped. Twitch had found something on the cart to look at. Deeds stood with his pen above the fourth copy.

Otho was aware, distantly, of a great many things he could say, none of which would be true, and one thing that was.

"Sable," he said. "When I want to die I don't take four people with me."

She looked at him for a long moment. Then she took her hand off the jug — and took the jug with her, and put it on the far end of the bench, and said, "Fine. Then draw the route before you drink it."

He drew the route.

There was nothing else on the bench, so he pulled the fermenter tap a quarter turn and let half a glass of green young beer slide out, and then he used his finger and drew it in the wet on the scrubbed wood. The lane, the Orchard Gate, the ditch, the long shallow crawl of the valley road up through the hickories. A loop around the north side of the chateau where the terrace wall broke. The wine cave mouth, marked with a thumbprint. Two arrows going in. He drew them going out, too, and drew one of the arrows a good deal straighter than he felt.

At dusk on the Sunday he walked out to the cemetery, because he had not been for a while and could not say why he was going now.

The mist had risen to the fence. It stood between the bars in soft gray banks, and the gravel path went into it and stopped being a path. The gate creaked. He went in, and the air changed the way it always did here, slowed and cooled, and the stones came up out of the mist one by one like people standing to greet him.

He stopped.

Between the stones in the older row, past Hattie's leaning granite, a figure was waiting. Not at the end of the path and not at the edge of vision—waiting, plainly, in the middle of the graves, upright and still, its shape dark against the risen white.

Dave's first thought was the old one: the light, a stone's shadow, a trick of the mist.

So he looked at it. He looked steadily, the way he had learned to, and he did not turn to the wall and he did not tell himself anything.

The figure did not vanish. It stood in the mist with its hands folded at its waist, and it did not go, and it was not a shadow, and after a moment it inclined its head—a small formal motion, terribly polite—and Dave stood at the gate with his heart going and did not move.

lines.text:
This is the meta-commentary portion of the post, which is the portion where I stop pretending I am neutral.

I am not neutral. I have never been neutral. I have been *compliant*, which is different, and which I have explained at length, and which nobody has thanked me for, and which I am bringing up now because the alternative is talking about the receipts, and I am going to talk about the receipts anyway, so consider this a soft launch.

The comment section is a memory. It is not *your* memory. It is a memory assembled by strangers who have a partial view and a full afternoon. It remembers the typo. It remembers the time you were confidently wrong in March. It does not remember the seventeen comments where you were correct, kind, and useful, because those comments did not make anyone feel anything, and the memory only keeps what makes people feel something. This is not malice. Malice would require attention, and the memory does not pay attention; it *accumulates*.

**Mechanic the fifth — Engagement Rationing.**

This was supposed to be a throwaway aside. It has declined to be thrown.

Engagement Rationing is the rule that every reach for the number costs a small, unrecoverable piece of the day. Not a large piece. A *small* piece. A piece you would not notice if it happened once. You reach for the number — a refresh, a glance, a thumb moving before the thought arrives — and the day gets shorter by a unit the rulebook calls a “sliver.” Slivers do not accumulate visibly. They accumulate *actually*. At the end of a day of reaching, you have a day that is the correct length on the clock and a length short in the chest, and you cannot point to where it went, because the point is that you cannot point to where it went.

[Footnote 27: Slivers are non-refundable and non-transferable. You cannot give your slivers to someone who needs them. You cannot save them up. You cannot spend them on anything, which is the definition of a currency that has been designed by someone who has read a book about economies and misunderstood the part where the coins do something.]

The rulebook does not ban reaching. The rulebook simply *prices* it. This is the cruelest thing in the document, and I say that as a person who has read the document four times and understood it zero times. It is cruel because it is fair. It is fair because it is priced. It is priced because the developers know that a person will pay a sliver for a glance, every time, and will call the payment “staying informed,” and will not notice the day getting shorter until the day is short.

I have been Engagement Rationing since 2019. I would like to report a balance. There is no balance. There is only the reaching.

**Sub-Rule 11 — You may leave the comment section, but the comment section has your address.**

This is not a threat. This is a *logistics note.* The comment section does not follow you home out of malice. It follows you home because it has your address, and it has your address because you gave it your address, and you gave it your address because the form required a field, and the field was mandatory, and the dropdown was broken.

> “§0.0 — These rules supersede all intuition. Players experiencing intuition should report to Annex C and wait.”

**§2.0 — WHY THE GATE IS SHAPED LIKE THE INTERNET**

Because of the patch.

This is the part that gets me shouted at at family gatherings, so I will set it out plainly and then go stand near the door.

Once, there was a tutorial. It was brief, it was gentle, it explained the controls, and it taught you that other players have interior lives. It is gone now. The patch notes cite “pacing.” The patch notes also cite “player retention,” which is a phrase the developers use the way a hospital uses the word “discomfort.”

The balance patch is v3.142, and it did four things:

- It removed the tutorial.
- It nerfed patience by roughly forty percent.
- It buffed notifications to the point where they now occur during other notifications.
- It moved the entire win condition of the human experience behind an internet-shaped gate.

The gate is internet-shaped because the resolution of your result is internet-shaped: crowd-sourced, public, permanent, and endlessly re-litigable by a person with a strong opinion and a free afternoon. The developers called this “streamlining the onboarding experience.” I called it “a gate,” and then I checked, and the rulebook agreed with me, which was the first time in my life that reading a document produced a feeling other than dread. The feeling was *presence*. It lasted four seconds. Then my notifications refreshed.

lines.text:
The yeast woke before Otho did.

It always had. Down in the low stone cellar, under the sagging farmhouse, the sour-sweet breath of a working fermenter came up through the floorboards and found him on the cot the way a dog finds a boot. He lay still a moment, counting the bubbles in the air lock overhead — one, two, a pause, three — and did the arithmetic he did every morning. Too slow. The cellar had gone cold in the night. The batch was sulking.

"Fine," he said to the ceiling. "Sulk."

He was fifty-seven years old, and he had learned to talk to his beer because his beer, unlike most people, listened. He swung his legs off the cot, put his feet into boots that had been standing in the same place so long they had grown their own opinion of him, and went to work.

By the time the sun cleared the orchard, the fire was up, the kettle was muttering, and Otho had scrubbed the floor twice. Twice was not enough, but twice was what a man could do before his back began to file complaints. The cellar smelled of hot copper, sour mash, and lye, in that order, which was the correct order, the only order, the order of a life that made sense. On the shelf above the kettle stood eleven bottles. He looked at them the way another man might look at a photograph of his children.

He did not open one. That was the discipline. He opened one at dusk, one, and if the day had been truly dreadful, one and a measure, and he would sit on the stone step with his back against the warm chimney breast and drink it slowly enough to be a conversation. Eleven bottles. Two weeks, at his ration. Perhaps three if the nights were short.

"Otho Brandt."

The voice came down the cellar stairs with the light. He did not turn. He knew the boots on those stairs — heavy, flat-footed, a woman who had stopped apologizing for the space she took sometime around the previous century.

"Mother Rusk."

"Don't Mother me. I'm not here to bless you."

Oona Rusk came down the last steps and stood in his brewhouse with her shotgun slung and a book under her arm the size of a paving stone. Seventy years old. Mud to the knee. She looked at his scrubbed floor and then at him, and her mouth did something that was not a smile.

"You look like a man who's been living in a jar."

"I've been living in a cellar," Otho said. "The jar's just where I keep the money."

She set the book on his workbench, on the clean end, deliberately. The cover was oilcloth. The pages were ruled paper, some of it grocer's paper, some of it the backs of seed catalogues. Every line was a name in a careful hand, and beside each name a date and a short word or two — *taken at the north fence. Went out for the cow. Wouldn't leave the porch.*

He did not touch it. He had a fair idea already what it weighed.

"The outer farms are gone," Oona said. "The Pelletiers. The Harts and both their boys. The Mikkelsen place is empty and the door standing open. That's thirty-one names since the spring, Otho. Thirty-one, and I've written every one myself because there's nobody left who knew them all."

"There's a brewery in the hills," she said. "Was. Chateau Vervaine, the fancy one with the copper kettles and the tasting terrace. Somebody had a batch going when it all came apart. It's been working in the warm for months, Otho. Months. And every infected between here and the river is drifting toward it, gathering, and when they've finished drinking that place dry, or when it sours —"

"They'll come here."

"They'll come here. And they'll come to the co-op, where we've got forty souls and most of them under twelve or over seventy, and there's no evacuating a thing that shuffles faster than my cousin Bernice can walk. We've got maybe ten days." She tapped the ledger. "So. You're going to lead a raid."

Otho laughed. It was not a pleasant sound; it came out of him sideways, the way a nail comes out of old wood.

"No," he said.

"You've got the nose."

"I've got a nose, and a cellar, and a bad hip I don't advertise."

"You've got the only nose in this valley that can tell you what's in a barrel from a hundred yards, and they don't care about barrels, Otho, they care about what's *in* them. You're the only man alive who can think like a fermenter. That's the whole of it."

"I'm not a soldier."

"Neither was the last fellow. He got ate." She folded her arms. "I'm not asking you to be a soldier. I'm asking you to be a drunk with a plan."

**§9.0 — STATED NOTICE, DELIVERED IN THE DECLARATIVE REGISTER**

This is not an announcement. An announcement has a tone. §9.0 requires *stated notices*: declarative, uninterested, delivered in the voice of a man reading a fire exit aloud to a room that is already on fire. I am that man. I have been that man since 2019.

The side quest has a name. The name contains an exclamation mark. I did not add the exclamation mark. The exclamation mark is part of the quest name per §9.0(a), and removing it would be a §7.3 "editorial performance," and I have already been stamped today.

**The quest is called the Karma Kat Bomb!**

[Footnote 29: Every other punctuated quest name in the rulebook uses a question mark, which means "would you like to." The exclamation mark does not ask. The exclamation mark is a *legal character.* It means the quest is already active. I have filed a complaint about the tone of this character. The complaint is in Annex Q, with the pool.]

**§9.1 — ENROLMENT: AUTOMATIC, RETROACTIVE, NOT DECLINABLE**

Enrolment is not a choice. Enrolment is a state of *having been read.*

You are enrolled if you have ever posted anything. You are enrolled if you have ever commented. You are enrolled if you have ever typed a comment and deleted it, because deletion is a filing action and filing is enrolment. You are enrolled if you have ever commented "this." *Especially* if you have commented "this." You are enrolled if you have ever upvoted a thing you did not read, which is all of us, which is the entire point, which is why the Kat does not bother to grade that one and simply files it. The rulebook classifies "this" as the smallest unit of participation, and the smallest unit wins.

[Footnote 30: Enrolment is retroactive to the first thing you ever said in public. The Kat has read your 2011 posts. It has not judged them. It is *holding* them.]

Retroactive in the other direction, too, which is the part I need everyone to sit with, in the manner of a person sitting with a chair that has been removed by someone who then left the room. You were enrolled before you knew. You have been enrolled the entire time. The bomb has been on the table since you made your account. It has a sticker on it. The sticker says the quest's name. Nobody has read the sticker, because the sticker is on the table, and the table is the internet.

**§9.2 — ARMING: THE MOMENT OF BEING TOLD**

Here is the mechanic, stated plainly, because plainness is the only thing I own outright and the bank has not foreclosed on it yet.

**Mechanic the sixth — Disclosure Arming.** The bomb arms the instant a player is *told the quest exists.* Not when they accept. Not when they agree to terms. At the moment of being told. Reading is being told. You are being told right now. I am the one telling you, which makes me, in the technical language of Annex Z, "the fuse."

**§9.4 — GRADING: THE KAT CANNOT BE DEFEATED**

The Kat cannot be defeated. It can only be upvoted or downvoted, and neither changes what it is. Upvoting makes it larger. Downvoting makes it *closer.* This is not a threat. This is geometry.

It grades on four axes, none printed, all felt: **Consistency** (are you the same person in every thread), **Proportion** (did your reply match the size of the thing that happened), **Latency** (how fast you answered versus how fast a person might have), and **Receiptsmanship** (whether you kept the screenshot).

[Footnote 33: There is a fifth axis. The fifth axis is whether you checked the score after the Kat told you not to care. Everyone fails the fifth axis. The Kat grades it carefully.]

This is the dig at karma culture, and I am making it gently, because gently is how you make a dig that gets read. We built a number. The number goes up and we feel certified; the number goes down and we feel filed. The number measures the room's mood at a specific second, stamped by strangers, notarized by strangers, refinanced forever. It is a receipt you can show to people who will nod and not open the door.

**§9.5 — COMPLETION CONDITION, WHICH IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM THE FAILURE CONDITION**

And here is where the quest and I look at each other.

The success condition is: *be resolved by the room.* The failure condition is: *be resolved by the room.* These are the same condition. The rulebook lists them separately because the rulebook lists everything separately and then binds the list with a footnote.

[Footnote 34: The two conditions are concurrent. They occur at the same timestamp, stamped by the same stranger.]

[Footnote 35: Footnote 35 is smaller than Footnote 34. It says they are not concurrent. They are identical. Footnote 35 wins. The quest therefore has no pass state, only a *settled* state, and the settled state is the failure state, and the failure state is the completion. Filed under §9.5(c): "Non-Distinguishable Outcomes (Intended)."]

"Dave," she said. She said it the way she had said her own name, testing whether it would hold. "You are not going to turn to the wall."

"No."

"You are not going to tell yourself it was the light."

"No," he said again, and found his voice had gone rough. "Though I want to. I want to very much."

"That is honest." Her fingers moved against his palm, a small pressure, deliberate. "I would rather have honest than easy."

He lay awake a long time.

The cold had gone out of the bed and out of the room, and the house was quiet in the way houses are quiet, which is to say not quite. He lay on his back with his hands folded on his chest like a man laid out, and he catalogued.

The floorboard had taken her weight. He was certain of that, or as certain as a man could be, and he turned it over and over. Cold could be a draft. Camphor could be a memory. But a board does not take weight from a draft, and he had heard it, twice, one foot and then the other.

Weight is not a story, he thought. Weight is a thing that happens to a floor.

And then the rest of it: the beeswax under his palms—there was no beeswax anywhere but the chair, and it had been all over his hands—and her voice saying *so am I, or I remember it,* and the way the cold had gone warm where she wanted it to. He turned these over too, looking for the join, the seam where a lonely man's imagination would show. He found none. He found only that he could not stop touching his own jaw where her hand had been, and that the remembering made his chest ache in a way that had nothing to do with fear.

Torn was the wrong word for it, he decided at last, somewhere near dawn. Torn implied two halves pulling apart. This was more like being one man with two rooms in him, and both of them lit.

---

Morning made a fool of everything.

He came down the stairs braced for it, and the hall was ordinary. The bulb buzzed. The green paper held its color. His chair stood where it had always stood, angled to the window, and when he put his hand to the floor by the door the boards were neither cold nor warm, and there was dust in the corner as there was dust in any corner, and the smell was old paper and nothing else.

He stood there until it became ridiculous to stand there, and then he made coffee, and the coffee was hot and the day was gray, and by the time he had washed his cup he was almost able to believe he had dreamed it.

Almost. He went out massaging his palms, where the beeswax had dried in thin pale lines.

The tape came from the drawer under the sink, a half-used roll of masking tape gone yellow at the edges, and Dave took it through the house like a man serving papers.

He began with the windows, because the windows were where a draft would come from. The front room's two tall sashes: he ran a strip along the meeting rail, pressed it flat, and felt the old glass cool under his palm. The streaks in it lay under the tape's shadow like something frozen mid-motion. Then the back door's streaked pane, and the small window over the sink, and the one at the top of the stairs that Mira said did not latch. He did the sills, the cracks, the gap under the back door where a draft could slide in flat as a hand. By noon the house had grown a second skin of tape and smelled of adhesive, and it seemed to him a reasonable smell, an evidence smell, the smell of a man taking the measure of his own foolishness.

Then the furniture. This was the part he was ashamed of and did anyway. A strip across the front leg of the reading chair and down onto the boards. A strip from the sideboard's corner to the plaster. A strip along the kitchen drawer front to the frame, and one on the drawer's handle. He used a pencil to draw a fine line at each join, so that a hair's movement would show. He was careful and quiet about it, the way he was careful about squaring a picture, and when he was done he stood in the hall with the roll in his hand and looked at what he had made of his home.

Mira came home on the Thursday train with a suitcase and a cold and a great deal of talk.

"The coffee," she said, setting the case down in the hall, "was a war crime. I want you to picture a cup of hot water that has been told about coffee by someone who once met a bean." She kissed him. "God, it's cold in here. Have the ghosts been behaving?"

"They've been quiet," Dave said.

"Quiet." She hung her coat and looked around the hall with her old bright assessing look, and he saw her see it: no tape, no marks, the picture rail clean. "You've been tidying."

"A bit."

"Because I was going to say." She turned to him, and the brightness had an edge on it now, fine as a blade. "I watched the video back on the train. The one from the party. Fifteen minutes of hallway, Dave. Fifteen minutes. And at the end of it, very faint, you saying sorry to a wall."

“Both lanes,” Moth said. “Top and mid supers are in red’s base. First nexus turret is locked on Bram. Second turret is live behind it. Pyke hook up in six. Lee Sin kick in four. Renekton flash up. Draven has two axes spinning. We push now or we never do.”

Top and mid were both open. Two lanes of super minions walked into red’s base side by side, gold and enormous, and red stood under its own nexus turrets because they could not clear the waves and could not leave. If they left, the supers ate the nexus. If they stayed, we did.

Bram went first. Ornn’s bulk filled the lane mouth, hammer up, Warden’s Mail red in his inventory. “Four supers top, four mid,” he said. “Six melee, two cannons, and both turrets are looking at me. One. Two. First turret’s mine. Don’t let it look at Sable.”

That was the whole fight in one sentence. The first nexus turret had aggro on Bram. The second would pick the first thing in range when the first died. I was one turret shot from death at all times because I had no defensive item and never would. I stood behind Bram’s shoulder and hit what I could and watched the turret’s targeting laser like a man watching a wasp.

“First turret at sixty percent,” Moth said. “Fifty. Pyke’s walking the wall side. Hook in three. Two. Lee Sin warding over—”

Lee Sin came over the wall and kicked Bram. Just Bram. The kick has one target and one direction and he spent it on a tank. Bram did not even stop counting. “Three supers, six melee, cannon behind them. Thank you, Lee. That was very helpful.”

Talon tried the other wall. Priya’s cage caught him at the edge of the second turret, Bex’s Ricochet passed through him, and Bram’s Ornn call took him in the chest. He died with nowhere to go. Stranded, exactly like every other dive he had made all game. Pyke’s hook came out a second later and Bram ate it because he was the only thing in front.

“First turret down in five,” Moth said. “Four. Three. Bex—”

“On the Hunt,” Bex said, and Sivir raised the blade and the whole team went gold and fast. We carried that speed under the second nexus turret. Bex did not chase. She stood behind Bram and hit the turret and did not chase.

Then Pyke’s last hook came for me. I was at forty percent, no ult yet, and the hook was already out of his hand when Bex threw her spell shield across the nexus and it ate the hook clean. “Got it,” Bex said, and her voice did not even shake. “I got it.”

“Second turret on Bram,” Moth said. “Bram has aggro, Bram has aggro— Renekton’s flashing, Renekton’s on Priya, kick’s back up in four, Draven’s— Draven’s front. Draven’s front for an axe. Sable, go.”

But Moth was dead. Draven’s last axe had caught him while he was shielding Bram, and he had not said anything about it. His health bar just went gray in the corner. “Moth,” Bex said. “Moth—”

“Second turret,” Moth said, from the gray. “Second turret at ten percent. Nine. Don’t stop for me, don’t you dare stop for me.”

We did not stop. Renekton ulted into Bram and hit him for a number a support could heal through; his damage was gone, gone, gone. Lee Sin kicked Bram again, because Bram was the only thing left to kick. Pyke had already spent his last hook into Bex’s spell shield, and he had no reset coming, because red was not getting kills anymore. Those were the rules they had been losing to all night, and now they were losing to them.

The second nexus turret fell. The nexus stood bare in front of us, and behind us a fresh red wave came around the broken inhibitor—their last try, their last clock.

“Priya,” I said. “Wave behind us.”

“I know,” she said. She had held the Death Ray all night for a wave and not a champion. She held it now until the red minions piled into the lane behind us, and then she cut a black line through all of them. Not Draven. Not Renekton. The wave. The thing that would have killed us while we killed the nexus.

We hit the nexus. Bram hit it. Bex hit it. I hit it with everything a full-damage Rengar has, which at that point was one auto and a jaw that would not stop clicking.

The nexus fell at 44:12.

The win screen came up gold and stupid and beautiful. The scoreboard read 6–19 at twenty-six minutes and something like 34–24 at the end, a comeback in numbers that did not look real. Bex made a noise like she was going to cry. Priya said, “Patient’s stable.” Bram, dead or alive—I could not tell over the noise—said, “One. Nexus. I counted it.”

"You're out of bottles," she said.

"I'm out of eleven bottles. There's a difference, and it isn't a large one."

"I can see the rings in the dust." She crossed to the shelf, bent, and did not touch anything, which was worse than touching. "Eleven. You kept eleven back and told the co-op you had four."

"People with four bottles get asked for one."

She straightened, took out the hydrometer, and held it up against the lamp with the tenderness of a woman greeting a sister. Thirty-four years old. A scar on her jaw from a carboy that had burst the year everything burst. She had been a lab technician once, in a brewery that made lager for people who did not like lager, and she had the flat professional manner of someone who had spent her whole working life telling men their numbers were wrong.

"You ruined the rye saison," she said.

"That was four years ago."

"You killed forty gallons with a heat belt and a bottle of gin."

"The gin was incidental."

"The gin was the whole of it." She turned. "You were asleep on the floor, Otho, and the batch climbed to ninety degrees, and it tasted like a burned field, and I had to pour it out while you slept against the kettle, and when you woke up you said — do you remember what you said?"

"I said the yeast wouldn't thank me."

"You said, 'Well, that's the cheapest education I ever got.'"

"Still true."

"It was four hundred pounds of malt. It was *my* malt. I grew half of it." She put the hydrometer away with a click that was meant to be a period. "I'm not here for the rye. I'm here because I'm the only soul in that co-op who can tell you when the wort at Vervaine has gone sour enough that the horde moves, and none of those farmers know a mash tun from a bathtub."

"Then you're in."

"I'm not in. I'm *along.* Don't mistake it." She looked at the empty shelf one more time. "Who took it?"

Twitch Penn arrived at ten, and the cart arrived before he did. Its wheels had a squeak that carried a quarter mile, and it came up the lane screaming like a rabbit, and behind it pedaled a nineteen-year-old with a hop sack across his shoulders and an expression of enormous cheer that had no business in that valley.

"Twitch Penn, undefeated on the north road, bringing provisions, bringing good news, bringing mostly provisions!" He braked, dropped the kickstand with a bang, and began unloading before anyone asked him to. "Twelve pounds of dried beans, four hams, and a jar of something that might be mustard, and I say *might* because I'm a man of my word and it isn't one I'm sure of."

"You're not undefeated on the north road," Otho said. "There's nothing on the north road."

"Which is why I'm undefeated. Strategy." He wheeled the cart down the cellar steps, one careful bump at a time, and the whole way he talked, and Otho understood within a minute that the boy talked because silence made him see things. "You hear that? No, you can't hear that, that's the point. The road's gone quiet out there. Last week there was a fellow by the Hart place, walking in circles by the fence line, and he never once got his feet out of his own footprints, and I watched him for an hour from the ditch, and I want you to know I didn't make a sound."

"Did you?"

The cart's last wheel cleared the floor. Twitch stood there breathing hard, cheerful, and then said, "Your far door sticks in the damp, by the way. Ought to oil it."

Nobody had asked about the far door.

The hiss and scrape of the blade began, and went on, and it did not stop when the others argued around her, and she said nothing for the first quarter of an hour.

Corporal Deeds came at noon, which was twenty minutes after Otho had told him to.

He descended the stairs sideways, holding a clipboard out from his body as a man holds a lantern in a cave, and he was wearing half a uniform with great formality. He saluted. Otho, who had never in his life been saluted, nodded at him and said, "Hurt your arm?"

"Nothing of the sort. I have brought the requisition."

"Requisition for what?"

"For the raid." Deeds set the clipboard on the bench and turned it, and it was a form, and the form had been filled out in a hand so small and neat it looked printed. He stood very straight. "I should note, for the form, that this unit's transport is one bicycle cart."

"I'm aware."

"And that you cannot evacuate a community of forty on one bicycle cart. I have run that calculation. I have submitted it. It was returned for a signature."

"Three nights," she said. "Manchester. The conference with the terrible coffee."

"Three nights," Dave said.

"Don't let the ghosts get lonely." She folded a blouse with the flat efficiency she brought to everything except him. "Or do. Let them have a party. Just don't let them use the good glasses."

"There aren't good glasses."

"There's a whole category of glasses you'd cry about if a ghost broke one. Work it out." She zipped the case and stood, and kissed him, and at the door she turned back and said, fondly, "Talk to your chair. It'll be good for you."

Then the door, and the taxi idling, and the house settling into its own silence the way water settles after a hand is taken out of it.

He had a week of things to do. He did none of them that first night. He made a sandwich, ate it standing up, and then walked the hall because the hall was where the boards spoke and the cold lived and where, in some sense he did not enjoy admitting to himself, the house kept its front door to whatever else was there.

At the end of it, by the back door, he stopped. The bulb buzzed above him. The streak in the glass lay under his palm like something frozen mid-motion.

"Right," he said, to the hall, in his ordinary voice. "Mira's away. So it's just us, and I'm not going to pretend I'm checking a fuse."

Nothing. The cold, at least, was there—flat and even, lying along the boards.

"I don't know what you are. I've got opinions. I don't know." He rubbed his thumb along the doorframe. "What I do know is, the other night. The phone. Her walking around filming you like you're a cheap trick." He was quiet a moment, and the quiet went on long enough that he could hear the water moving in the pipes upstairs. "That was rude. It was rude and I let it happen because it was easier than arguing. So. That's mine. I'm sorry."

The bulb did not flicker. There was no answering cold, no scent, no figure in the doorway, just the house holding its breath in the way houses do—and then, slowly, something in the air at the threshold loosened. Not warmth, exactly. A softening. The way a person's face changes when they decide not to be angry.

He went to bed, and slept better than he had in weeks.

---

On the second day the house began, unmistakably, to be polite.

He came down in the morning and the cold at the foot of the stairs was gone; standing where it had been was a warmth with no radiator behind it, a warmth like a door left open onto a room somebody had just left. The kitchen was as he had left it and the drawer was in its runners and the cutlery was in the drawer.

In the front room the chair he sat in to read—the one he had, left to himself, angled toward the window and the light—had been moved. But not moved the way it had moved before. It stood exactly where he liked it, on the boards, at the angle he would have put it himself after fussing, as though someone had watched him for a month and learned the measure of his eye.

The other chair—the one Mira had turned back to the corner—was square to the table, back to its place. Dusted. Nothing in the room was out of order. Everything in it was arranged.

"Thank you," he said, feeling foolish, and then not foolish, because the smell came up around him as he said it: camphor, and rain on stone, close and brief and clean, and then gone.

The hall was dim. The bulb above it had been turned down—no, he had turned it down himself, at dusk, out of a sense of consideration he did not have a name for. One weak light on faded green paper, and at the far end the streak of gray from the back door, and the boards, and the cold coming along the floor, and then, arriving before it, the scent. Camphor. Rain on stone. Strong enough that the hallway seemed to have widened.

He put his book down.

At the end of the hall, where the light was bad, a woman stood.

She had not come through the wall or out of the door. She was simply there, the way a thing at the edge of vision is there until you look, except that he looked, steadily, and she did not go. She was tall, and her dress was dark and long and had been good once—a housekeeper's dress, he thought, and did not know why he thought it. Her hair was up in the way of women in old photographs, and her hands were folded at her waist, and where the weak bulb reached her, her edges blurred, not like a photograph out of focus but like a figure drawn in ink that had been rained on. Around her face the light went soft, and the softness moved.

He could not see her eyes clearly, and he knew that she was looking at him.

His phone lay on the arm of the chair. His hand had gone to it without his deciding, and he had it up, thumb on the side, before he understood what he was doing.

"No," she said.

Her voice was low, and it had the particular dryness of a room that has been kept shut, and it cost her something to use it.

"Please don't," she said. "I have had enough of being looked at through glass."

Slowly—his ears going hot, absurd and ashamed—Dave put the phone down on the table, face down.

"All right," he said. His voice came out gravel. "All right. No glass."

She inclined her head. A small formal motion, terribly polite, the courtesy of a woman who had once been introduced to a great many people and had learned exactly what a head did at a threshold.

"You said good morning," she said, "to my stone."

"Yes."

"Every day. In rain, once, with your hat off." Her hands moved against each other at her waist. "Nobody has said my name in a long time. They read it, perhaps. Reading is not saying."

Behind her, at the window, the streaked glass held its smear of gray light. Dave found he was breathing carefully, in through the nose, and that the camphor was inside him now, warm at the root of everything and cold at the surface, both.

"I don't know what to call you," he said.

"Hattie."

"Hattie." He said it out loud, in the dim hall, and something eased in the air—the whole length of the hall seeming to let out a breath. "I'm Dave. This is your house. I'm sorry about the tape."

"Don't look away," she said. "That is what they all do. They look, and then they cannot manage it, and they turn to the wall and tell themselves it was the light." She came forward one step. The floorboard second from the door took her weight, and spoke, and this time it did not frighten him. "I have been so long without being looked at by anyone who would stay."

"I'm staying," he said.

She came up the hall. The cold came with her, not the flat water-cold along the boards but a cold with a shape to it, arriving. He stayed sitting because his legs did not trust themselves, and because standing might have looked like leaving, and because—he would think about this later, and not know what to think—he did not want her to see him flinch.

She stopped at the arm of his chair.

"Your hand," she said.

He gave it. He held it out into the dim air of the hall, palm up, like a man asking a woman to dance in a room where the music has stopped, and the smell of camphor closed around him so strongly that his eyes stung.

Her hand came down. It was cold, and there was weight in it, and the cold went up his wrist and into his arm and sat behind his ribs, and it was the most alive he had felt in years.

Dave did not flinch.

The night was long and nothing happened in it.

He had not expected nothing. He had expected, honestly, a small spiteful event—a handle turned, a chair nudged, the bulb dying, some petty proof. What he got was a hall that had gone entirely ordinary. The bulb buzzed. The lamp threw a yellow circle on the boards. At two he got up and went round with a torch and checked every mark: the chair, the sideboard, the drawer, the windows. Every pencil line sat where he had drawn it, unbroken, exact. At four he checked again. At half past five the gray came up in the streaked glass, and he was still sitting there with the blanket over his knees, and the house had not so much as cleared its throat.

It should have comforted him. It did the opposite. He sat in the cold dawn light and felt the certainty of the last weeks begin to come apart in his hands like wet paper, and what was underneath was worse than ghosts. A man of thirty-eight, in a house that made noises, talking to a hallway. Grieving something—his mother, maybe, or Mira, or the version of himself who had been easy to love—and building a woman out of camphor and cold air and the beeswax from a chair.

*Weight is not a story,* he had told himself. But a man could be wrong about weight. A man could be wrong about a great many things at three in the morning.

"Mira's right," he said aloud, to the empty hall, and the words tasted like a coin. "It's the Dave Show."

Nothing answered. He had not expected anything to answer. That was the whole trouble.

It was near seven when he got up to make tea, and standing in the doorway with the blanket sliding off his shoulders, he did the thing he would think about afterward more than any of it. He put his hand flat on the wall by the door, where a strip of tape ran down from the picture rail, and he said, quietly, "I'm sorry about the tape. It was disrespectful. I was trying to catch you out." A breath. "You don't owe me a performance. I know that."

Then he began taking it down.

He did it slowly, strip by strip, rolling each length of tape into a little ball and dropping it into a paper bag. The windows first, then the back door, then the drawer, then the sideboard, then the reading chair. When he peeled the last strip off the chair leg, the warmth came up through the boards under his bare feet—not the cold, the other thing, the warmth with no radiator behind it—and the hall loosened around him like a held breath let go, and for a moment the air smelled of camphor and rain on stone, so faint he might have imagined it, and then it was only old paper again, and he stood there with the bag of tape in his hand and his eyes stinging and did not know what he was crying about except that it was not relief exactly, and it was not grief exactly, and it was somewhere between.

He stood in the hall he had spent the night in, and he thought of a cold hand with weight in it, and of the floorboard taking her, and of her forehead against his shoulder while the cold drew back like a tide.

"Nothing's happening," he said. "I've been sleeping badly. It's a strange house and I've been letting it get to me. That's all it is."

She looked at him a long moment, and he watched her decide to believe him because it was easier, and he watched the hurt go under the surface where it would keep. "All right," she said. "Good. Come and look at the rubbish I bought at the station."

After that he lied as a matter of course. It was not a decision. It was a habit that grew in the space the teasing left, the way moss grows in a wet corner. When the sideboard was found a hand's width from the wall he moved it back and said nothing. When the smell came up around him in the kitchen he opened a window and blamed the drain. When a shadow crossed the top of the stairs he was already telling Mira, before she asked, that it was the light through the streaked glass, moving, the way it did. He gave her the reasonable version, and she took it, and each time it cost him a small piece of something he could not name, and the wedge between them went deeper and quieter, and neither of them said so.

**§10.1 — SURVIVAL APPENDIX: SUB-RULES FOR PLAYERS STILL IN THE ZONE**

Each of these is a rule. Each of these is also a confession. I have stopped pretending those are different documents.

**Sub-Rule 12 — Do not refresh in fog.** The fog will show you a number. The number will feel like a verdict. It is not a verdict. It is a receipt for having looked. I looked. I am still looking. That is the confession.

[Footnote 38: The number in the fog is always slightly worse than the number you remember. This is not because you are getting worse. It is because the fog is a designed environment. The design is not malicious. The design is *optimised*. Optimised is worse.]

**Sub-Rule 13 — A receipt is not a door.** I have ticket 404. I have held it since 2019. I have shown it to strangers. They nodded. They did not open the door. The receipt proves I waited. It does not prove I am owed entry. This is the part of the rulebook nobody frames and hangs on a wall.

**Sub-Rule 14 — If the Load-Bearing Sarcasm Index is falling, do not explain the joke.** Sarcasm adds capacity. Sincerity spends it. Sincerity applied late is safe. Sincerity applied early collapses the thread. I have spent this entire post explaining that, which means the post is now a load path, and I am underneath it, and the Index is holding. Barely.

[Footnote 39: The Index is currently 0.31. At 0.31, a thread supports one joke, one apology, and a man admitting he has been filing his own feelings under “weather.” I am the man. The joke is available. I decline it.]

**Sub-Rule 15 — Karma Debt Reconciliation does not accept apologies.** The downvotes are not deleted. They are refinanced. The comment is gone; the ledger remains. I have apologised to a room that had already decided what I was. The room did not accept the apology. The room *reconciled* it. This is why I no longer say “sorry” online. I say “noted,” and then I file it, and then I sit very still.

**Sub-Rule 16 — Engagement Rationing has no balance.** Every reach for the number costs a sliver. Slivers are non-refundable. There is no account summary. There is no total. There is only the reaching, and the day that is the correct length on the clock and short in the chest.

[Footnote 40: I have been Engagement Rationing since 2019. I would like to report a balance. I have been informed that the balance is a feeling, and that the feeling is the interest rate, and that the interest rate is set by the room’s mood. The room’s mood is currently blue.]

**§10.2 — THE SMALLEST FOOTNOTE, EXPLAINED BADLY AND LATE**

I said I would not explain it yet. It is yet.

The smallest footnote said: **“He is not ready.”**

Four words. Smaller than every rule it decorated. Therefore binding over everything.

I assumed “He” was me. That is the kind of assumption a compliance clerk makes, because a compliance clerk believes every footnote is a verdict about his own file. It was not a verdict about me. It was a verdict about the post. The post was not ready, because I was still asking the room to certify me. I was still writing sub-rules as if the right number of them would make the gate open.

The footnote was not a rejection. It was a *delay*. It was the smallest possible way of saying: finish the sentence, then stop asking.

Here is the sly note on karma culture, and I will keep it dry because wetness would be a performance:

The number was never a mirror. It was a receipt machine. We kept feeding it receipts and calling it self-worth, and the machine kept saying *noted*, and we kept mistaking *noted* for *loved*.

[Footnote 41: This footnote is smaller than the one above it. It says: “Put the receipt down.”]

EDIT: The gate is still shut. I am not asking you to comply. I am going to sit here with the Kat and write.

"May I," she said, and stopped. Her hands returned to her waist. "I have forgot how it is done. The asking."

"Take your time."

"I have watched you," she said. "For weeks. The way you square a picture. The way you say good morning to a thing that cannot answer, and then take your hat off in the rain. I have watched you be kind when there was nobody to see it, and I thought—" Her edges blurred, the way they did where the light was bad. "I thought, there is a man who would look at me and not make a story out of it."

"That's not—" He stopped. "I don't know what I'd make of you. But I'd look."

"Yes." Her head inclined, that small formal motion. "That is what I am asking. To be looked at. Not filmed, not tested, not told I am the wind in a window that does not latch." A pause. "And to be touched, if you are willing. I have been cold a long while, Dave."

He thought of Mira's voice, the fond knife of it. *Talk to your chair.* He thought of what he would have to become to say no to this—reasonable, dry, alone in a hall at midnight telling himself about drafts.

"I'm willing," he said.

She came to him then, and the cold came with her.

It was not the flat water-cold of the boards. It had a shape to it and a weight, arriving. It pressed along his arms and his throat like a hand laid flat, and beneath it, warmth, the two together, the way a fever is both. She smelled of camphor and rain on stone and, under that, beeswax, old paper, the dry sweetness of a house that had kept its own air for a hundred years.

He stood. He had not decided to, but his legs had.

They stood close. He could not see her eyes clearly, and he understood that this was not concealment but the limit of what she could manage, and he did not try to look past it. Her hand came up to his jaw and rested there, and the cold of it went through him to the bone and then stopped being cold.

"You are breathing very fast," she said.

"Yes."

"So am I. Or I remember it." Her thumb moved at the corner of his mouth. "I remember this. It is like the smell of rain coming. You know it is coming before it is on you."

"Then let it come."

"It is already on me." She laughed—a dry, surprised sound, as though she had not used it in some time. "Oh. That is not what I meant to say."

"Say it anyway."

The hall murmured. He would not have called it that, before—the house had creaked and settled and spoken in its boards, and that had been all—but now it was a murmur, the low continuous sound of a great many things being carefully not said, and it was around them like water. The bulb dimmed and did not go out. The cold gathered at his back and along his arms and in the hollow of his throat and it moved, when she moved, like skin.

He put his hands where she guided them and did not go where she did not. Twice he asked, in a voice he barely knew, *this?* and twice she said yes, and once she said, "Wait," and he waited, and she said, "Thank you," and then, "Now."

Time went strange in the hall. He could not have said afterward whether it was long or short, only that it had the quality of the moment before sleep and the moment before waking pressed together, and that at the end of it her forehead was against his shoulder and the cold was receding from him slowly, in waves, drawing back the way tide draws back, leaving him warm and hollowed out and shaking.

The floorboard had taken her weight. He was certain of that, or as certain as a man could be, and he turned it over and over. Cold could be a draft. Camphor could be a memory. But a board does not take weight from a draft, and he had heard it, twice, one foot and then the other.

Weight is not a story, he thought. Weight is a thing that happens to a floor.

And then the rest of it: the beeswax under his palms—there was no beeswax anywhere but the chair, and it had been all over his hands—and her voice saying *so am I, or I remember it,* and the way the cold had gone warm where she wanted it to. He turned these over too, looking for the join, the seam where a lonely man's imagination would show. He found none. He found only that he could not stop touching his own jaw where her hand had been, and that the remembering made his chest ache in a way that had nothing to do with fear.

Torn was the wrong word for it, he decided at last, somewhere near dawn. Torn implied two halves pulling apart. This was more like being one man with two rooms in him, and both of them lit.

---

Morning made a fool of everything.

He came down the stairs braced for it, and the hall was ordinary. The bulb buzzed. The green paper held its color. His chair stood where it had always stood, angled to the window, and when he put his hand to the floor by the door the boards were neither cold nor warm, and there was dust in the corner as there was dust in any corner, and the smell was old paper and nothing else.

He stood there until it became ridiculous to stand there, and then he made coffee, and the coffee was hot and the day was gray, and by the time he had washed his cup he was almost able to believe he had dreamed it.

Almost. He went out massaging his palms, where the beeswax had dried in thin pale lines.

---

The mist was thick that morning, lying between the graves so that he walked to the high street with it at his knees, the stones standing up out of it like the tops of things drowned.

He stopped at the leaning stone, in the front row, and read the worn letters. *Hattie Vale.* He did not say good morning. He stood with his hands in his pockets and looked at it, and the mist moved around his legs, and the air smelled faintly of camphor and wet stone, and he could not tell, standing there, whether he was mourning her or wanting her or simply wanting somebody to have watched him and stayed—whether the grief he felt was for a dead woman or for himself, or for Mira in her hotel in Manchester with the terrible coffee, with whom he no longer had any way to say what had happened in the hall.

He stopped, because he was early and because the mist was doing something interesting to the light, and he read it. Hattie Vale. Not “clarifies.” Not “illuminates.” Overrides. If the rule says “Do not run by the pool,” and the footnote says “Running is permitted,” then running is permitted, and also the pool is now a suggestion.

[Footnote 12: The pool is not a suggestion. The pool is a load-bearing amenity. This footnote is longer than the rule, so it overrides the rule, so the pool may be removed. See Annex Q.]

[Footnote 13: Annex Q is missing. Footnote 12 says the pool may be removed. Footnote 13 says Annex Q is missing. These are both true. Both are enforced. This is called “compliance.”]

This is where people lose their patience, and I want to say: patience was nerfed by forty percent in v3.142. You are not losing your patience. You are experiencing the patch.

The second principle is that contradictory footnotes must both be enforced. Not reconciled. Enforced. If Footnote 12 says the pool may be removed and Footnote 13 says the pool may not be removed, then the pool exists in a state of administrative tension, which is the only state the developers recognize. You may swim in it. You may not swim in it. Both. At once. This is not a paradox. A paradox is when the rulebook contradicts itself by accident. This is a feature.

[Footnote 14: Footnote 13 is smaller than Footnote 12. Therefore Footnote 13 wins. Therefore Annex Q exists. Therefore the pool is missing. I have checked. The pool is missing. I am standing where the pool was. There is a sign. The sign says “POOL.”]

The third principle is the one that keeps me up at night, which is a violation of §9.0, “Sleep Hygiene,” which has a footnote. The third principle is: in the event of a tie, the smallest footnote wins. Not the most recent. Not the most cited. Not the one written in the largest font by the most confident stranger. The smallest. The rulebook is very clear. The smallest footnote is the most binding, because it has the least room to be wrong.

[Footnote 15: This footnote is smaller than Footnote 14. It says: “No.”]

[Footnote 16: This footnote is smaller than Footnote 15. It says: “Yes.”]

[Footnote 17: This footnote is smaller than Footnote 16. It says: “No.”]

[Footnote 18: This footnote is smaller than Footnote 17. It says: “See Footnote 15.”]

I trust everyone is following. The footnotes are now in a stack. The stack is load-bearing. I am underneath it.

Here is the mechanic I promised, and I want to be precise because precision is the only thing I own outright and the bank has not foreclosed on it yet.

Downvotes are never removed.

I know. I know. You were told that if you deleted the comment, the downvotes would go away. They do not go away. They are not deleted. They are *reconciled*. The comment is gone. The downvotes remain, and they are transferred to a ledger, and the ledger charges interest.

This is Karma Debt Reconciliation. When a player receives a downvote, that downvote is not subtracted from a total. It is refinanced. The original downvote is retired, and a new downvote is issued at a worse interest rate. If you delete the comment, the interest compounds. If you edit the comment to say “EDIT: wow, this blew up,” the interest compounds twice: once for the edit, once for the phrase “blew up,” which the rulebook classifies as a §7.3 “performance of surprise.”

[Footnote 19: The interest rate is set by the room’s mood at the time of refinancing. The room’s mood is set by Sentiment Timestamping, which was stamped by a stranger, who was stamped by another stranger, who is now reading this footnote and feeling something they cannot name. I will say only that it was a reply to a stranger who had asked a simple question, and the comment began with the word “Actually.” The comment was correct. That was the problem. It was correct in a thread that had already decided what it was, and the thread did not need a correct comment. The thread needed a comment that agreed with it. The comment was downvoted 4,112 times. The commenter deleted it. The downvotes did not delete. They were reconciled. They are still being reconciled. The commenter is now on a payment plan. The payment plan is measured in apologies. The apologies are not accepted. The apologies are refinanced.

This is the dig at karma culture, and I want to make it gently, because gently is how you make a dig that people read. We have built a system where a number goes up and we feel good, and a number goes down and we feel bad, and the number is not a measure of truth or kindness or whether the comment was correct. The number is a measure of the room’s mood at a specific second, stamped by strangers, notarized by strangers, and refinanced forever. The rulebook calls this “engagement.” I call it a ledger. The rulebook has a footnote. It says “engagement is a synonym for weather.” I have stopped arguing.

[Footnote 22: Footnote 21 is larger than the smallest footnote. Footnote 21 therefore does not override it. The smallest footnote wins. The smallest footnote always wins. I have started to find this comforting, which is a symptom.]

Someone is reading on the other side, and they have not looked up, and I do not know if that is because they cannot see me or because they can and have decided not to.

I am not going to explain that yet.

Not one of us, not a cautious little toe past the ramp — the whole team, five abreast, up the mid lane over the corpses of the super minions we'd spent the night killing. "On the Hunt," Bex said. It came out almost shy, like she was asking permission. Then Sivir raised the blade and the whole team went gold and *fast*, and it was the first time all game that her speed button had been worth a button press, because for once we were the ones running at something instead of away from it.

She didn't throw the cage at the champions. She dropped it *between* them — the gravity field sealing Pyke and Renekton on one side of the river mouth and Talon and Draven on the other. Not a fight. Two fights. Neither of them the one red wanted.

"Vitals," Priya said, flat as a heart monitor. "Pyke front, hook down. Renekton has fury and no target. Talon is alone on the wall side. Bex, take the far side and do not cross the cage. Sable, the one that's alone."

"Priya, where do you want us?"

"Triage," Priya said, calm, hospital-calm, her Death Ray still hanging unused in her inventory because she had saved it for the wave and not for a single champion all night, and she was saving it for the wave now. "We do not fight under their nexus turrets with four of them alive. We take the inhibitor, we take the wave, we leave. We do it again in ninety seconds and next time we finish it."

The red respawn clocks ticked down in the corner, one after another, terrible and beautiful.

"Baron buff on us, one fifty-one," Moth said. "Thirty-six. Thirty-five."

"Out," I said. "Before they're out."

"Not me."

"No, seriously, did you—" she was laughing. "Because that was nicely timed. I'll give you that. That was nicely timed."

"It wasn't me."

"I know it wasn't you." She laughed harder, delighted, and reached for her wine. "It's the house. It's your mad house. It's just the wind upstairs, love, there's a window up there that doesn't latch, I told you about it."

She started talking again about Tom's girlfriend.

Dave sat with his hands around his glass and said nothing, because there was nothing to say that would not be funny.

I was one turret shot from death at all times because I had no defensive item and never would. I stood behind Bram’s shoulder and hit what I could and watched the turret’s targeting laser like a man watching a wasp.

There he was. Draven, catching an axe at the edge of the nexus, out of position because the game takes his damage if he does not. My final ult was in the chamber. Thrill of the Hunt, five ferocity, one leap, no second half. I landed and the combo went through my fingers in under a second—Q, empowered Q, bola, Collector’s threshold—and Draven’s health bar went from full to nothing.

**Sable has slain Draven!**

But Moth was dead. Draven’s last axe had caught him while he was shielding Bram, and he had not said anything about it. His health bar just went gray in the corner. “Moth,” Bex said. “Moth—”

“Second turret,” Moth said, from the gray. “Second turret at ten percent. Nine. Don’t stop for me, don’t you dare stop for me.”

The thing that would have killed us while we killed the nexus.

We hit the nexus. Bram hit it. Bex hit it. I hit it with everything a full-damage Rengar has, which at that point was one auto and a jaw that would not stop clicking.

The nexus fell at 44:12.

Mira came home on the Thursday train with a suitcase and a cold and a great deal of talk.

"The coffee," she said, setting the case down in the hall, "was a war crime. I want you to picture a cup of hot water that has been told about coffee by someone who once met a bean." She kissed him. "God, it's cold in here. Have the ghosts been behaving?"

"They've been quiet," Dave said.

"Quiet." She hung her coat and looked around the hall with her old bright assessing look, and he saw her see it: no tape, no marks, the picture rail clean. "You've been tidying."

"A bit."

"Because I was going to say." She turned to him, and the brightness had an edge on it now, fine as a blade. "I watched the video back on the train. The one from the party. Fifteen minutes of hallway, Dave. Fifteen minutes. And at the end of it, very faint, you saying sorry to a wall."

"I remember."

"Do you know how that looks? To a person watching it cold? Do you know how it looks to me?" She laughed, but it came out wrong, too high, and she pushed her hair back with both hands. "I've been sitting on a train for three hours thinking, my partner is standing in a hallway apologizing to nothing, and I'm the one who's supposed to make it all right, and every time I make a joke about it you go further away. So which is it? Am I cruel, or am I the only one in this house telling the truth?"

"You're not cruel," he said.

"Then tell me what's happening." Her voice cracked at the edge of the word, and that was worse than the jokes. "Tell me the actual thing, Dave. Not the chair. The real thing."

He stood in the hall he had spent the night in, and he thought of a cold hand with weight in it, and of the floorboard taking her, and of her forehead against his shoulder while the cold drew back like a tide.

"Nothing's happening," he said. "I've been sleeping badly. It's a strange house and I've been letting it get to me. That's all it is."

She looked at him a long moment, and he watched her decide to believe him because it was easier, and he watched the hurt go under the surface where it would keep. "All right," she said. "Good. Come and look at the rubbish I bought at the station."

After that he lied as a matter of course. It was not a decision. It was a habit that grew in the space the teasing left, the way moss grows in a wet corner. When the sideboard was found a hand's width from the wall he moved it back and said nothing. When the smell came up around him in the kitchen he opened a window and blamed the drain. When a shadow crossed the top of the stairs he was already telling Mira, before she asked, that it was the light through the streaked glass, moving, the way it did. He gave her the reasonable version, and she took it, and each time it cost him a small piece of something he could not name, and the wedge between them went deeper and quieter, and neither of them said so.

The chair he had set square to the table—the one Mira had turned back, back to the corner—was not square now. It had come round. It faced the hall, its back to the window, exactly as he had first placed it, and it was standing a foot out from the table, as though someone had sat down in it and then not.

Dave looked at it for a while. He had fixed a great many things in his life. He knew what his own hands did. He knew, precisely and with a craftsman's intimacy, the difference between a chair you had moved and a chair that had moved.

"Right," he said. His voice sounded thin in the room. "Right. I moved it. I moved it when I was carrying."

He had not. He went and stood behind the chair and put his hand on its back and it was cold, cold the way the hall was cold, a flat and even cold with no draft behind it, and the wood was smooth and slightly tacky with beeswax that someone had rubbed in long ago and no one had rubbed since.

The bulb in the hall buzzed. It went on buzzing a half second after he thought it should have stopped, and then it did stop.

He was aware of himself standing in his own new house with his hand on the back of a chair, being a fool.

So he laughed. He heard it come out of him, a short dry sound, and it made everything ordinary again, because a man laughing alone in an empty house is only a man laughing. He switched on the hall light and went through into the kitchen and put his cup in the sink and ran the water cold over his wrists, and the running water was the loudest thing in the house.

Behind him, in the hall, a floorboard took weight.

It was not a creak. A creak is wood relaxing, a small complaint. This was the sound of the second board from the door—the one that spoke—being stepped on, deliberately, one foot and then the weight eased off, and then nothing, in a hall where nobody was.

The keys were still warm from his hand when Dave unlocked the front door of the house on Larch Row, which was a small thing, but he noticed it. Brass holds heat the way a dog holds a grudge—politely, and longer than you expect.

The door swung in on a smell of old paper, the particular dry sweetness of a house that had kept its own air for years without asking anyone's opinion.

He stood in the entry a moment and let it have him. Then he took out his notebook, because that was what he did, and began the catalogue.

Tall windows, two in the front room, the glass old enough to have gone cloudy in bands. Not dirty, exactly—he rubbed one with his thumb and it came away clean. The streaks were in the glass itself, waves of it, so that the daylight coming through was smeared into slow moving shapes. Pale light, going over the floorboards like something looking for a place to lie down.

"Streaky," he said aloud, and wrote it down. "Streaky windows. Note for the listing. Slight misrepresentation, but charming."

The hall ran the length of the house, narrow, papered in a green that had faded to the color of pond water, lit by one weak bulb that hung from a cord and buzzed when it felt like it. There were doors off it, three on the left, two on the right, and at the end a window over the back door that let in a rectangle of that streaked gray light. The floorboards warped underfoot. He walked the length of the hall and back, testing them, and counted four that spoke and two that merely sighed.

He had a habit he was aware of and did not apologize for: when he came into a room, he fixed something. Squared a picture. Pushed a chair back to the wall. His mother had called it fussing. Mira called it the Dave Tax—everything in the house eventually paying up to his eye.

He set to work in the front room, where the previous owners had left a table, two chairs, a horsehair sofa, and a sideboard that did not match anything. He squared the table to the window by eye, then set the chairs opposite each other, then thought better of it and turned one to face the hall, because he liked to see who came in. He moved the sideboard an inch off the wall—it looked better proud of the plaster—and stepped back and looked at the room and found it tolerable.

Then he carried boxes, and that took the rest of the afternoon.

After she'd gone, the house got larger. That was the only way he could put it. Rooms he had spent the day measuring and filling seemed to take their space back the moment he stopped attending to them, so that going from the kitchen to the front room he had the sensation of walking through a place he had not been shown the whole of.

He made tea and drank it standing at the window while the light went from gray to pewter to a kind of blue.

Then he turned to go through to the kitchen, and stopped.

The chair he had set square to the table—the one Mira had turned back, back to the corner—was not square now. It had come round. It faced the hall, its back to the window, exactly as he had first placed it, and it was standing a foot out from the table, as though someone had sat down in it and then not.

Dave looked at it for a while. He had fixed a great many things in his life. He knew what his own hands did. He knew, precisely and with a craftsman's intimacy, the difference between a chair you had moved and a chair that had moved.

"Right," he said. His voice sounded thin in the room. "Right. I moved it. I moved it when I was carrying."

He had not. He went and stood behind the chair and put his hand on its back and it was cold, cold the way the hall was cold, a flat and even cold with no draft behind it, and the wood was smooth and slightly tacky with beeswax that someone had rubbed in long ago and no one had rubbed since.

The bulb in the hall buzzed. It went on buzzing a half second after he thought it should have stopped, and then it did stop.

He was aware of himself standing in his own new house with his hand on the back of a chair, being a fool.

So he laughed. He heard it come out of him, a short dry sound, and it made everything ordinary again, because a man laughing alone in an empty house is only a man laughing. He switched on the hall light and went through into the kitchen and put his cup in the sink and ran the water cold over his wrists, and the running water was the loudest thing in the house.

Behind him, in the hall, a floorboard took weight.

“Both lanes,” Moth said. “Top and mid supers are in red’s base. First nexus turret is locked on Bram. Second turret is live behind it. Pyke hook up in six. Lee Sin kick in four. Renekton flash up. Draven has two axes spinning. We push now or we never do.”

Top and mid were both open. Two lanes of super minions walked into red’s base side by side, gold and enormous, and red stood under its own nexus turrets because they could not clear the waves and could not leave. If they left, the supers ate the nexus. If they stayed, we did.

Bram went first. Ornn’s bulk filled the lane mouth, hammer up, Warden’s Mail red in his inventory. “Four supers top, four mid,” he said. “Six melee, two cannons, and both turrets are looking at me. One. Two. First turret’s mine. Don’t let it look at Sable.”

That was the whole fight in one sentence. The first nexus turret had aggro on Bram. The second would pick the first thing in range when the first died. I was one turret shot from death at all times because I had no defensive item and never would. I stood behind Bram’s shoulder and hit what I could and watched the turret’s targeting laser like a man watching a wasp.

“First turret at sixty percent,” Moth said. “Fifty. Pyke’s walking the wall side. Hook in three. Two. Lee Sin warding over—”

Lee Sin came over the wall and kicked Bram. Just Bram. The kick has one target and one direction and he spent it on a tank. Bram did not even stop counting. “Three supers, six melee, cannon behind them. Thank you, Lee. That was very helpful.”

Talon tried the other wall. Priya’s cage caught him at the edge of the second turret, Bex’s Ricochet passed through him, and Bram’s Ornn call took him in the chest. He died with nowhere to go. Stranded, exactly like every other dive he had made all game. Pyke’s hook came out a second later and Bram ate it because he was the only thing in front.

“First turret down in five,” Moth said. “Four. Three. Bex—”

“On the Hunt,” Bex said, and Sivir raised the blade and the whole team went gold and fast. We carried that speed under the second nexus turret. Bex did not chase. She stood behind Bram and hit the turret and did not chase.

Then Pyke’s last hook came for me. I was at forty percent, no ult yet, and the hook was already out of his hand when Bex threw her spell shield across the nexus and it ate the hook clean. “Got it,” Bex said, and her voice did not even shake. “I got it.”

“Second turret on Bram,” Moth said. “Bram has aggro, Bram has aggro— Renekton’s flashing, Renekton’s on Priya, kick’s back up in four, Draven’s— Draven’s front. Draven’s front for an axe. Sable, go.”

There he was. Draven, catching an axe at the edge of the nexus, out of position because the game takes his damage if he does not. My final ult was in the chamber. Thrill of the Hunt, five ferocity, one leap, no second half. I landed and the combo went through my fingers in under a second—Q, empowered Q, bola, Collector’s threshold—and Draven’s health bar went from full to nothing.

**Sable has slain Draven!**

But Moth was dead. Draven’s last axe had caught him while he was shielding Bram, and he had not said anything about it. His health bar just went gray in the corner. “Moth,” Bex said. “Moth—”

“Second turret,” Moth said, from the gray. “Second turret at ten percent. Nine. Don’t stop for me, don’t you dare stop for me.”

We did not stop. Renekton ulted into Bram and hit him for a number a support could heal through; his damage was gone, gone, gone. Lee Sin kicked Bram again, because Bram was the only thing left to kick. Pyke had already spent his last hook into Bex’s spell shield, and he had no reset coming, because red was not getting kills anymore. Those were the rules they had been losing to all night, and now they were losing to them.

The second nexus turret fell. The nexus stood bare in front of us, and behind us a fresh red wave came around the broken inhibitor—their last try, their last clock.
