lines.text:
Good morning, afternoon, or whatever timezone the server believes you are in.

I am u/ComplianceGoblin_3142. I am a volunteer compliance clerk for the universe. I am not affiliated with the developers, I am not paid, I have not been asked to do this, and I will not be taking questions. I will, however, be taking corrections, and I will be filing them directly into the bin marked *Corrections*, which is the bin beside the other bin, marked *Questions*.

I am posting this in a subreddit that did not request it, which is the correct venue. A comment section is not a place where rules are read. A comment section is a place where rules are *encountered*, usually sideways, usually at 2 a.m., usually by a stranger who has decided you are That Kind Of Person. This is by design. I will get to that.

[Footnote 1: “Emergent property” is developer language for a thing that happens on its own and cannot be measured, defined, promised, scheduled, or complained about, but *can* be charged for. A close cousin of the emergent property is the “known issue,” which is a bug the developers have decided to call weather.]

I want to be clear that I am not criticising the rulebook. The rulebook is fine. The rulebook is load-bearing. What I am doing is *explaining* the rulebook to a comment section, which is like explaining tides to a bucket.

Before anyone comments — and someone will comment, because the comment section is a weather system and I am a person standing in it without an umbrella — I want to clarify what compliance means here. Compliance is not agreement. Compliance is the act of being measurable. The rulebook does not require you to like the gate. It requires you to be resolvable at the gate. This is why the gate has a queue, and why the queue has a sign reading NOW SERVING: EVERYONE EVENTUALLY, and why the sign has a footnote that says 'Eventually is not a unit of time.' I have stood in that queue. I have held the ticket. The ticket number was 404. I do not know what that means and I have decided not to investigate. Investigation is Annex R. Annex R is missing. The person who was supposed to staff Annex R has been reassigned to Annex Q, which is also missing, which is at least consistent.

**§1.1 — WHAT “RESOLVES” MEANS, ROUGHLY, IN PUBLIC**

Your Internet result does not resolve in private. There is no private. Resolution happens in the open, over time, in front of witnesses, and it is recorded. Two mechanics do the heavy lifting here, and I want to name them because unnamed mechanics are how people end up shouting.

**Mechanic the first: Sentiment Timestamping.** Every interaction you have online is stamped with the mood of the room at that exact second. The stamp is notarised. The notary is a stranger. The stranger is also being stamped. There is no appeal window and no receipt you can lose, because the receipt is other people.

**Mechanic the second: Presence Certification.** To be *considered* present at the door of The Human Race, a sufficient number of strangers must independently declare you mathematically present. Your own declaration counts for nothing. Your own declaration counts for less than nothing — the rulebook classifies self-declaration under §7.3, “Noise,” and §7.3 has a footnote too.

[Footnote 2: §7.3’s footnote reads, in full: “Yes, this includes you.” I have written to the developers about the tone of this footnote. I received an automated reply. The automated reply said “Yes, this includes you.”]

**§3.0 — ON COMMENT SECTIONS, WHICH ARE LOAD-BEARING**

People ask me — nobody asks me — why the rulebook permits comment sections at all.

The answer is in the structure. A comment section is not the game. A comment section is the *loading screen*. It is where the universe checks whether you can remain a person while being read by strangers. Most of us cannot. I certainly cannot. I have been in the loading screen since 2019.

I have tried closing the loading screen. The loading screen has a small x in the corner. The x is decorative. The rulebook explains this in §3.1(c), “Closure of Interfaces,” which states that any interface may be closed once, after which it reopens with a notification asking whether you are sure. You are never sure. The “sure” button is greyed out until you have consulted the comment section, and the comment section is the loading screen. This is what the developers call a loop. I call it a Tuesday. I have asked the x for a meeting. The x has declined.

And the reply guy. The reply guy is not a bug. The reply guy is architecture. Somewhere in the rulebook there is a clause about load-bearing structures that may not be removed without a permit, and I have decided the reply guy is one of them, because the alternative is that the developers simply enjoy this, and I am not prepared to file that.

**§4.0 — WHAT COMES NEXT, WHICH I AM NOT ALLOWED TO SAY**

There is a side quest. It has a name, and the name has an exclamation mark in it that I did not add, and it forces every enrolled player into the Internet Endgame Zone, which has no exit signs and lighting the colour of a screen at 3 a.m.

I am not unveiling it in this post. I have been advised not to. The advice came from me, and I took it very seriously.

[Footnote 3: I have read this rulebook four times. I have understood it zero times. I want to be honest about that, because the alternative is pretending, and pretending is a §7.3 violation, and I have already been stamped today.]

The batch was sulking.

"Fine," he said to the ceiling. "Sulk."

He was fifty-seven years old, and he had learned to talk to his beer because his beer, unlike most people, listened. He swung his legs off the cot, put his feet into boots that had been standing in the same place so long they had grown their own opinion of him, and went to work.

By the time the sun cleared the orchard, the fire was up, the kettle was muttering, and Otho had scrubbed the floor twice. Twice was not enough, but twice was what a man could do before his back began to file complaints. The cellar smelled of hot copper, sour mash, and lye, in that order, which was the correct order, the only order, the order of a life that made sense. On the shelf above the kettle stood eleven bottles. He looked at them the way another man might look at a photograph of his children.

He did not open one. That was the discipline. He opened one at dusk, one, and if the day had been truly dreadful, one and a measure, and he would sit on the stone step with his back against the warm chimney breast and drink it slowly enough to be a conversation. Eleven bottles. Two weeks, at his ration. Perhaps three if the nights were short.

He turned back to his kettle. The wort had come to the boil and the smell of it rolled up, sweet and grassy, and out in the orchard the wind carried it off toward the road, and he thought — the way he always thought, the way he could not stop thinking, it being the deepest thing in him — *that'll travel.*

"No," he said, and then, "Not the way you mean. I won't take your farmers and your boys and get them killed for a keg. But I'll do it. My way, my terms, my people, and when I say run, you run, and when I say leave the beer, you leave the beer. That last one won't be popular."

This was supposed to be a throwaway aside. It has declined to be thrown.

Engagement Rationing is the rule that every reach for the number costs a small, unrecoverable piece of the day. Not a large piece. A *small* piece. A piece you would not notice if it happened once. You reach for the number — a refresh, a glance, a thumb moving before the thought arrives — and the day gets shorter by a unit the rulebook calls a “sliver.” Slivers do not accumulate visibly. They accumulate *actually*. At the end of a day of reaching, you have a day that is the correct length on the clock and a length short in the chest, and you cannot point to where it went, because the point is that you cannot point to where it went.

[Footnote 27: Slivers are non-refundable and non-transferable. You cannot give your slivers to someone who needs them. You cannot save them up. You cannot spend them on anything, which is the definition of a currency that has been designed by someone who has read a book about economies and misunderstood the part where the coins do something.]

The rulebook does not ban reaching. The rulebook simply *prices* it. This is the cruelest thing in the document, and I say that as a person who has read the document four times and understood it zero times. It is cruel because it is fair. It is fair because it is priced. It is priced because the developers know that a person will pay a sliver for a glance, every time, and will call the payment “staying informed,” and will not notice the day getting shorter until the day is short.

I have been Engagement Rationing since 2019. I would like to report a balance. There is no balance. There is only the reaching.

“Get out,” Priya said.

“Second inhibitor,” Priya said. She sat back in her chair; I could hear it. “And two lanes of supers.”

He came down on Tuesday and the handles on the kitchen drawers were reversed—every one of them, the little brass pulls turned to the other side of the drawer fronts, so that you reached for them and found smooth wood. He stood a moment with his hand in the air. Then he took out his screwdriver and turned them all back, one by one, and did not mention it to anyone.

On Wednesday the lamp that lived on the sideboard in the front room was at the far end of the hall, on the floor by the back door, unplugged, its cord gathered in a neat coil.

On Thursday he was coming out of the kitchen with a plate and saw, through the doorway into the hall, a figure cross it. Not a shape in the streaked glass—a figure. Dark, upright, moving with the unhurried pace of someone who had somewhere to be and did not want to be hurried. It crossed the doorway from left to right and was gone.

He put the plate down and went into the hall and looked. The hall was empty. The bulb buzzed. There was cold there, the same flat even cold he had felt in the chair's back, and it lay along the floorboards like water in a low place, and he stood in it with his arms prickling and looked at the empty green hall and felt, absurdly, that he had interrupted something.

He told Mira that evening.

She was on the sofa with her feet tucked under her, scrolling, half listening in the way she had, and he told her about the drawer handles and the lamp and the figure, and she laughed—not unkindly, that was the thing, not unkindly at all—and said, "It's the Dave Show. This house has gone to your head."

"It's not a show. I'm telling you what happened."

"I know, love. I know." She reached up and patted his cheek without looking away from her phone. "You and your leaning gravestone lady."

"I didn't tell you about the gravestone."

"You did. You told me about the gravestone." She looked up then, grinning. "You said she had a good lean."

"There's a brewery in the hills," she said. "Was. Chateau Vervaine, the fancy one with the copper kettles and the tasting terrace. Somebody had a batch going when it all came apart. It's been working in the warm for months, Otho. Months. And every infected between here and the river is drifting toward it, gathering, and when they've finished drinking that place dry, or when it sours —"

"They'll come here."

"They'll come here. And they'll come to the co-op, where we've got forty souls and most of them under twelve or over seventy, and there's no evacuating a thing that shuffles faster than my cousin Bernice can walk. We've got maybe ten days." She tapped the ledger. "So. You're going to lead a raid."

Otho laughed. It was not a pleasant sound; it came out of him sideways, the way a nail comes out of old wood.

"No," he said.

"You've got the nose."

"I've got a nose, and a cellar, and a bad hip I don't advertise."

"You've got the only nose in this valley that can tell you what's in a barrel from a hundred yards, and they don't care about barrels, Otho, they care about what's *in* them. You're the only man alive who can think like a fermenter. That's the whole of it."

"I'm not a soldier."

"Neither was the last fellow. He got ate." She folded her arms. "I'm not asking you to be a soldier. I'm asking you to be a drunk with a plan."

"The part about the warm." He was already moving, up the steps, out into the yard, and the light hurt his eyes, and the wind came over the fence and hit him full in the face, and it was there, unmistakable, sweet and buttery and alive and faintly rotten at the edges, the smell of a hundred thousand gallons of wort working itself to death in a warm room. It came on the wind out of the hills. It would come on the wind all the way down the valley, and behind it, patient as weather, would come the shuffling.

"It's still working," he said. "God help us, it's still warm. They built a brewhouse a hundred years old with stone walls and no windows in the cellar. It'd hold heat like a fist."

"Can you use it?"

He stood in his own yard, breathing the smell of the thing that was going to kill everyone, and did the arithmetic. A warm batch pulls them. A cold one doesn't. Sugar makes them frantic; beer quiets them, for a while. He thought about casks, and about the difference between a man who runs from the horde and a man who makes the horde run to the wrong place.

"No," he said, and then, "Not the way you mean. I won't take your farmers and your boys and get them killed for a keg. But I'll do it. My way, my terms, my people, and when I say run, you run, and when I say leave the beer, you leave the beer. That last one won't be popular."

So he stood with his back to the sink and told her, plainly, with nothing in his voice arranged to make her laugh. The cold at the back of the chair in October. The drawer handles. The dark figure crossing the doorway from left to right. Hattie at the end of the hall, her voice dry as a room shut up for years, asking him not to look at her through glass. The hand with weight in it. The floorboard taking her, one foot and then the other. The beeswax dried in pale lines on his palms, which he had stood and looked at in the morning light until looking became a kind of answer.

"And the rest," he said. "The part I didn't tell you at the grave. One night in November she came to me in the hall and I didn't send her away. It wasn't nothing. I'm not going to make it nothing to make this easier for one of us."

She did not laugh. She sat very still, and her face moved slowly through several things, and when she spoke her voice was low. "You've never said it like that."

"Like what?"

"Like you were telling me the weather."

"The lies were mine," he said. "Every one. The drain, the window, the light through the glass. I told you those because it was easier than watching you decide I was a fool. That was cowardice, and it cost you more than it cost me."

"I said choose," she said. "In the graveyard. Me or the house, tonight." She looked at her cold cup. "I meant it. And I don't know what I meant by it. I don't see anything, Dave. I stood there and the air went wrong and something moved and I still can't get my head around a woman in a hall." She pressed the heel of her hand against her eye. "And I've been horrible. Not the jokes—the jokes I could defend. The way I used them. I teased you because it was easier than believing you were lonely in a way I couldn't get at. Every joke made me the one who was fine. I liked being the one who was fine."

"You weren't to know."

"Don't do that. Don't be gracious at me." She almost smiled, and stopped herself. "I don't know what's real in this house. I know what I felt in that mist. I know I put my hand on your sleeve and couldn't make my voice work. That's as far as I get."

Mira was at the front door with her coat on and the door shut, which meant she had not decided to leave. Morning came through the streaked glass in slow cloudy bands and lay across the floor and up the wall.

"I'm not going to choose," Dave said. "I know that's not what you asked. But I won't stand in a doorway and say the house isn't what it is to keep you, and I won't say you aren't what you are to keep it. The only choice I've got is whether I tell you the truth."

"I know," she said. "I've been thinking about it since six. It's a stupid ultimatum. I made it because I was frightened and because it let me be the reasonable one." She looked at the window and the light lying in bands. "I still don't believe it. I want that written down. I don't believe it."

"No."

"But I believe you." She said it carefully, as though testing the boards of it. "That's different, and it's the best I've got tonight, and it might take me a while to get anywhere else with it."

"That's enough to be going on with."

"It might not be, some days."

Here is the proof. Six sub-rules. Each one dumber than the last. That is not a flaw. That is an audit trail.

**Sub-Rule 1 — You may not win The Internet while explaining The Internet.**

I want everyone to sit with this one, in the way one sits with a chair that has been pulled out from under them by a person who then leaves the room.

[Footnote 4: This sub-rule was added in v3.141 after a player attempted to win The Internet by posting a 9,000-word explanation of how The Internet is won. The attempt was ruled "instructionally sincere," which is a category that exists.]

**Sub-Rule 5 — A typo is a permanent felony. A war is a "reply."**

I did not write this sub-rule. I checked. I checked twice, which is once more than the rulebook requires and once fewer than the comment section will demand.

The classification schedule is in Annex Y, which is not missing, which is the problem. Per Annex Y:

- "teh" — permanent. Unappealable. Follows you to the Human Race lobby and is read aloud at the door by someone who is not judging you, they are *just noting* it.
- "should of" — first-degree, with a mandatory reply from a stranger who is not angry, they are *just asking*.
- A leaked document containing the coordinates of a hospital — a "reply."
- The statement that a war is occurring — a "reply," possibly a "hot take," appealable only by being correct in a thread that has already decided what you are.

[Footnote 9: The rulebook's position is that a typo is *durable* because it can be quoted forever, whereas a war is *contextual* because it can be reclassified as a "discussion" once enough people have posted "source?" beneath it. Footnote 9 is longer than Sub-Rule 5. Footnote 9 therefore overrides Sub-Rule 5. Sub-Rule 5 no longer exists. I have left it in for tone.]

**Sub-Rule 6 — All rules are subject to the smallest footnote.**

I have lost the thread.

That is a technical term. Therefore I am renumbering.

**Sub-Rule 7 (formerly Sub-Rule 6, which was formerly Sub-Rule 5, which is now vacant and will not be filled, because filling it would require me to remember what it was, and I have looked, and I do not.)**

Sub-Rule 7: A player who has lost the thread must say so in the thread. This is the only sub-rule never broken, because breaking it requires you to notice you have broken it, and awareness is the one resource the patch did not nerf.

I am aware. I am saying so.

That is compliance. Not agreement. Compliance.

He had not meant to come. He had meant to walk past, the way he did every evening now, on the long way home from the high street with a bag of groceries growing heavy in his hand. But the figure was there, waiting in the older row past Hattie's leaning granite, upright and dark among the risen white, hands folded at its waist.

He stopped at the gate and did not go in. He had learned that much. There was a way of doing this—the looking, the steady looking, the small courtesy of not pretending—and there was a way that took, that pushed, that asked for more than was being offered. The figure waited to be recognized, not approached. So he recognized it: a dark head inclined slightly, an acknowledgment given and returned, and then the shape thinned into the mist like breath drawn back into a body.

He went in then, and walked the front row, and found the stone.

It leaned harder than its neighbors, as it always had, and the mist had wet it dark. He crouched and put his fingers in the carved letters, which was easier than reading them, and read them anyway. HATTIE VALE. And below, where the dates had gone soft, the shapes of numbers he had only ever guessed at. But this dusk the light lay flat and cold across the granite, and the shapes resolved, the way a word resolves when you stop squinting at it.

Eighteen ninety-one. Nineteen twenty-three.

He stayed crouched a while with his hand on the stone. It was not a revelation. It was worse than a revelation; it was a confirmation, a small click in the lock of the world, and behind it the whole house on Larch Row rearranged itself. The streaked windows. The boards. The hand that had weight in it. Nineteen twenty-three. She had died in that house, or near enough to it that the two places had kept the same cold. The grave and the hallway were the same address now, and he had been walking between them every day of his life for months, and never once had he thought to look at the numbers.

"All right," he said to the stone, quietly. "All right, Hattie."

Mira let go of his sleeve and stepped back from the grave.

"Right," she said. Her voice was shaking, and she made it steady by force. "Right. We're going home. We're going home now, and we're going to talk, properly, and then—" She stopped, and looked at him, and he saw her make the decision he had been dreading. "Then you're going to choose. Me, or that house." She nodded at the leaning stone, at the whole quiet mist of it. "Because I'm not doing this. I'm not living with a man who hears a dead woman's name in the floorboards. So. Me, or the house and everything you say it holds. Tonight, Dave."

She turned and walked toward the gate, and her footsteps were loud on the gravel, and the mist opened for her and closed behind her.

Dave did not follow.

He stood in the front row with his hand still on the leaning stone, and the mist kept its own weather around him, and he stayed, and did not answer, and the name was still in his mouth—Hattie, Hattie—and the cold had gone out of the ground, and behind him, up at the fence, Mira waited with her back to him and her arms folded and did not call his name again.

**§7.0 — SUB-RULE 8: THE NUMBER IS NOT A MIRROR, IT IS A WEATHER REPORT**

I am going to say something now, and I want to say it in the least inflammatory way available to me, which is to say it in the second-least inflammatory way, because the least inflammatory way is silence and silence has never once been filed correctly.

Here it is. I am not making a dig at karma culture. I am *noting a system property*. A dig implies intent. I have no intent. I have a clipboard.

The property is this: a stranger can reduce you to a number, and then you will check the number, and the number will become your mood. Not *reflect* your mood. Become it. This is not a metaphor either. I have watched a man — me, in the reflective surface of a dark monitor at 2:41 a.m. — refresh a figure that does not love him back, and I have watched his face do a small thing, a fractional thing, a thing too small to photograph and too large to forget, and that face was the face of a person doing arithmetic about his own worth with a calculator someone else is holding.

That is not a dig. That is a *description of the calculator.*

[Footnote 24: The calculator is held by strangers. The strangers are holding calculators too. Nobody has put the calculators down. There is no clause permitting the calculators to be put down. I have asked. The clause about putting things down is in Annex Q.]

I am aware of how this reads. I am aware that a post which says “I am not making a dig” is, structurally, a dig wearing a lanyard. I have considered removing the sentence. I have decided to leave it in, because removing it would be editing, and editing compounds interest, and I have already explained the interest.

**Sub-Rule 9 — The comment section remembers what you wish it would forget, and forgets what you wish it would remember.**

This is the meta-commentary portion of the post, which is the portion where I stop pretending I am neutral.

I am not neutral. I have never been neutral. I have been *compliant*, which is different, and which I have explained at length, and which nobody has thanked me for, and which I am bringing up now because the alternative is talking about the receipts, and I am going to talk about the receipts anyway, so consider this a soft launch.

**Mechanic the fifth — Engagement Rationing.**

This was supposed to be a throwaway aside. It has declined to be thrown.

Engagement Rationing is the rule that every reach for the number costs a small, unrecoverable piece of the day. Not a large piece. A *small* piece. A piece you would not notice if it happened once. You reach for the number — a refresh, a glance, a thumb moving before the thought arrives — and the day gets shorter by a unit the rulebook calls a “sliver.” Slivers do not accumulate visibly. They accumulate *actually*. At the end of a day of reaching, you have a day that is the correct length on the clock and a length short in the chest, and you cannot point to where it went, because the point is that you cannot point to where it went.

[Footnote 27: Slivers are non-refundable and non-transferable. You cannot give your slivers to someone who needs them. You cannot save them up. You cannot spend them on anything, which is the definition of a currency that has been designed by someone who has read a book about economies and misunderstood the part where the coins do something.]

The rulebook does not ban reaching. The rulebook simply *prices* it. This is the cruelest thing in the document, and I say that as a person who has read the document four times and understood it zero times. It is cruel because it is fair. It is fair because it is priced. It is priced because the developers know that a person will pay a sliver for a glance, every time, and will call the payment “staying informed,” and will not notice the day getting shorter until the day is short.

I have been Engagement Rationing since 2019. I would like to report a balance. There is no balance. There is only the reaching.

And then I heard it.

Not a notification. Not a refresh. A *purr* — low, warm, structured, the way a sound is structured when it has been designed by someone who wants you to keep listening. It came from the edge of the post. The edge of the post is not a place a sound should come from. The edge of the post is a margin. Margins are where footnotes live and where nothing else is permitted, per §6.0, which is load-bearing, and which I have quoted.

I know what the sound is. I have known since Footnote 23. The Karma Kat has read this post, and it is still waiting for the disclosure, and now it is purring, which is not a word the rulebook uses, and which I am therefore classifying as weather.

I should stop writing. That is the compliant action. That is the action a clerk takes. I have the form. The form is greyed out.

I am going to keep writing.

[Footnote 28: I am aware this is the wrong decision. I am aware that a person who hears a purr at the edge of his own post and continues typing is not a compliance clerk, he is *content*, and content is a §7.3 category, and I have been stamped today. I am aware. I am saying so. That is compliance. Not agreement. —The OP, who would like it noted that he is fine, and who would like the record to show that he hesitated, and who would like it very much if the record did not show how briefly.]
